sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) studies agents that iteratively revise their own designs based on experience (Hu et al., 2025; Zelikman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b). Agent harness evolution offers concrete form of this idea for language-model agents: it keeps model weights fixed while persistently changing the surrounding system that shapes observations and turns model outputs into actions (Lin et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026c). Depending on the harness, these changes can target prompts, skills, tool interfaces, orchestration, or source code, going beyond static prompting and memory-based Preprint 1 Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution adaptation (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Recent frameworks close the loop between execution, diagnosis, mutation, and evaluation, reporting gains on standard benchmarks (Hu et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). These benchmark gains suggest that harness evolution is promising avenue for pursuing RSI. However, higher overall benchmark score do not mean more useful agent. It averages over tasks and trials, so newly solved tasks can conceal lost ones, while deployment cost and performance beyond the tasks that guided evolution remain unseen (Gao et al., 2026; Kapoor et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b). Relying on that score alone can favor brittle or expensive agent versions and mistake adaptation to the tasks used during evolution for general improvement. Meaningful progress instead requires gains that are reliable across tasks, affordable to deploy, and effective on tasks that did not guide evolution. We aim to explain which persistent harness changes produce useful gains and how evolution generates and preserves them. We organize our empirical investigation around three research questions: RQ1 (Phenomenology): Does agent evolution yield reliable and efficient improvements, or does it suffer from task-coverage trade-offs and hidden costs? RQ2 (Generalization): Do the gains achieved during evolving survive when the agent is deployed in novel environments or tasks? RQ3 (Mechanisms): How do specific evolutionary operators contribute to the generation and preservation of beneficial modifications? We study AHE (Lin et al., 2026a), HyperAgents (Zhang et al., 2026c), A-Evolve (Lin et al., 2026b), and GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) with MiniSWE (Yang et al., 2024) and Codex (OpenAI, 2026) on τ3-Banking (Shi et al., 2026) for general tasks and Terminal-Bench 2 (Merrill et al., 2026) for coding tasks. Repeated evaluations compare evolved and initial agents in reliability, empirical coverage, regressions, and deployment cost. Split and cross-benchmark comparisons assess generalization, while controlled expansion of existing agents, change interventions, and admission replays trace how gains arise and persist. Fig. 1: The agent harness evolution procedure (left) and our analyses of Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms (right). Harness evolution redistributes task success, with new coverage accompanied by regressions 2 Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution across harnesses, task domains, and evolution paradigms. The practical value of these gains depends on deployment cost and whether they persist beyond the tasks that guided evolution. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, yet combining them can alter their value. The strongest existing agent need not offer the greatest further improvement, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Useful improvement therefore requires productive starting points, compatible changes, and search decisions that preserve gains. We connect these findings to operator redesign as constructive follow-up. Analyses of Phenomenology, Generalization, and Mechanisms jointly guide revision hypotheses for select, analyze, mutate, and gate. Each hypothesis specifies its supporting evidence, expected effects, and applicability conditions. We combine these revisions into Audit-Guided Evolution (AGE) to test their practical value. Our contributions can be summarized as: Revisiting Practical Improvement. We reveal gap between benchmark gains and practical utility, showing that useful improvement in agent harness evolution requires preserving useful behavior, managing deployment cost, and sustaining gains beyond the tasks that guide evolution. Understanding the Fragility of Gains. We identify productive agent selection, change compatibility, and search retention as central challenges. Current performance can misrepresent further improvement potential, useful changes can interfere, and admission can discard stronger versions. Improving Evolution Through Analysis. We translate these findings into coordinated revisions of diagnosis, mutation, selection, and admission. The resulting AGE algorithm improves reliability and coverage over its reference method across both benchmarks and harnesses. 2. Related Work Agent Optimization and Evolution. Agent improvement spans inference-time refinement, optimization of persistent artifacts, and open-ended self-modification. Reflexion retains linguistic feedback in episodic memory across trials, whereas Self-Refine iteratively revises the current output (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). ReflectEvo trains small language models on self-generated reflections to improve introspection and reasoning (Li et al., 2025). RAM learns from communications to improve an external memory system (Li et al., 2024), and The AI Hippocampus surveys implicit, explicit, and agentic memory mechanisms (Jia et al., 2025). DSPy optimizes language-model programs, and TextGrad propagates textual feedback through computational graphs (Khattab et al., 2024; Yüksekgönül et al., 2025). Promptbreeder evolves both task and mutation prompts, ACE maintains evolving context playbooks, and CoEvoSkills co-evolves multi-file skill packages with separate surrogate verifier (Fernando et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a, 2025b). The four approaches examined here make different choices within this space. AHE exposes editable harness components and uses distilled execution evidence to guide revisions (Lin et al., 2026a). HyperAgents makes both the task agent and its modification procedure editable (Zhang et al., 2026c). A-Evolve frames deployment-time adaptation as goal-directed optimization over persistent system state (Lin et al., 2026b). GEPA combines trajectory reflection for prompt updates with Pareto selection of complementary candidates (Agrawal et al., 2026). Harness and Program Evolution. Related approaches also optimize system structure and executable code. GPTSwarm optimizes prompt-bearing graph nodes and orchestration edges, while AgentSquare searches combinations of planning, reasoning, tool-use, and memory modules (Shang et al., 2025; Zhuge et al., 2024). ADAS uses meta agent to generate agent programs (Hu et al., 2025). Self-modification extends to the improvement procedure itself: STOP revises optimizer scaffolding, 3 Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution and the Darwin Gödel Machine evolves its own coding agent (Zelikman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b). AlphaEvolve instead evolves target algorithm programs using executable evaluation feedback (Novikov et al., 2025). Recent work also explores optimizers that construct their own optimization pipelines (Xue and Yang, 2026). RSIHub composes evolution methods from reusable operators and provides shared evaluation and lineage tracking (Wang et al., 2026c). This distinction between improving task solutions, agent implementations, and optimization procedures motivates separating what changes from how those changes are generated and retained. Capability Boundaries and Mechanisms. Empirical studies of reasoning distinguish improved small-k success from expansion of large-k task coverage (Yue et al., 2025). Token-level analyses identify concentrated learning signals at high-entropy decisions (Wang et al., 2025a), while studies of onpolicy distillation examine behavioral compatibility and information novelty (Li et al., 2026). Related work also examines the feedback used for improvement. UAPO introduces uncertainty-aware utility anchors for preference optimization (Wang et al., 2025b), and SAVE uses value-anchored on-policy feedback to update reward models (Wang et al., 2026a). We apply related analytical perspective to persistent agent-system changes rather than model-weight updates. Repeated evaluations distinguish reliability from empirical coverage, common-process Parent expansion tests improvement potential, Component interventions examine change compatibility, and frozen-pool admission replays assess retention. Evaluation of Agent Systems. Agent evaluation must account for cost, reproducibility, and generalization beyond aggregate success (Kapoor et al., 2025). For harness evolution specifically, Wang et al. (2026b) find inconsistent advantages over test-time scaling under comparable feedback and inference budgets, together with limited held-out generalization. Performance also depends on interactions among the model, harness, task structure, and coordination overhead (Kim et al., 2025). The τ-bench family emphasizes reliable tool-agent-user interaction, while Terminal-Bench 2 evaluates long-horizon execution in terminal environments (Merrill et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025). We study general and coding tasks through these complementary settings, distinguish task exposure during evolution, and assess external transfer without further agent revision. These comparisons connect measured improvement to its deployment cost and scope of applicability. 3. Preliminaries 3.1. Definitions An agent = (M, H) consists of frozen model and harness H. Evolution Process and Methods Methods and Harnesses. We evaluate AHE (Lin et al., 2026a), HyperAgents (Zhang et al., 2026c), A-Evolve (Lin et al., 2026b), and GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) using GPT-5.4. AHE and HyperAgents are implementation-centric recipes that emphasize agent engineering, whereas A-Evolve and GEPA are reflection-centric recipes that distill execution feedback into reusable changes. We run each recipe with two harnesses. MiniSWE 2.4.5 (Yang et al., 2024) is source-editable and permits inner-source changes. Codex 0.143.0 (OpenAI, 2026) is outer-layer-only and permits changes to prompts, skills, configuration, and external orchestration. These combinations let us examine different evolution designs under common process. Appendix details their implementations. In this common process, each recipe specifies how seven operators are implemented: select chooses Parent, rollout collects execution evidence, analyze diagnoses it, and mutate proposes Candidate. The validate operator optionally checks the proposal, gate decides admission, and record archives outcomes. We focus the mechanism analysis on select, analyze, mutate, and gate because their decisions determine which Parents are used, how evidence guides changes, and which Candidates persist. sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Experiments run in isolated benchmark environments rather than live user-facing services. Evolving agent instructions and code can introduce regressions and unintended tool use. We retain fixed evaluation contracts and harness-specific editing permissions, and examine regressions and transfer alongside aggregate performance. Participants in the human evaluation provided informed consent. The expert-review protocol evaluates the evidence, reasoning, and proposed approaches for operator revisions, as described in Appendix E.2. Neither benchmark gains nor expert endorsement establishes safety for deployment.

It considers whether to retain, revise, or roll back the preceding change and pursue different explanation. change manifest records the proposed mechanism, affected files, predicted fixes, and behaviors at risk. Debugger reports supply hypotheses for revision. There is no separate optional validate stage. The gate operator admits completed, eligible evaluation without requiring higher score, so the next Parent can come from lower-scoring revision. The record operator preserves outcomes and change evidence. Admission and continuation are thus distinct from final Champion reporting. A.2. HyperAgents Selection and Evidence. HyperAgents permits revision of the improvement procedure as well as the target agent (Zhang et al., 2026c). Its initial select policy samples eligible Parents using scoredependent weight and penalty for having many children. Higher scores increase sampling weight, while the child-count penalty reduces repeated expansion of the same Parent. The rollout operator reuses Parent evaluation traces. The initial analyze operator supplies metrics and browsable raw traces, leaving their interpretation largely to the mutation agent rather than first producing AHE-style debugger reports. Revision and Admission. Mutation may change the target and permitted operator implementations while leaving the evaluator and other fixed contracts unchanged. The mutation instructions favor substantive target changes but allow an operator-only revision when the evidence supports process-level change. An operator revision takes effect at its next invocation, updating the initial policies in Table 11 for subsequent Generations. The initial validate stage checks Python syntax in target files and the mutation operator. The initial gate admits completed, eligible evaluations without Parent-relative score threshold. The record operator stores lineage experience, including the Parent, outcome, and score. This editable search procedure distinguishes HyperAgents from target-only revision under fixed operators. A.3. A-Evolve Selection and Behavioral Feedback. Our A-Evolve implementation operationalizes experience-driven adaptation (Lin et al., 2026b). The select operator chooses the highest-scoring eligible Parent, and rollout collects fresh Train trajectories. The analyze operator compresses observable behavior, including tool use, repeated actions, errors, and completion signals, for trajectory-only judge. This judge evaluates behavior without benchmark reward labels. Its proxy judgments provide feedback for revision, rather than replacing the benchmark score used for admission. Revision and Admission. The mutate operator distills these observations into reusable task-solving guidance and executable target changes. Its instructions emphasize recurrent failure patterns, selfcontained skills with their supporting dependencies, and preservation of unrelated behavior. Prompt and skill settings organize revision within the Harnesss legal editing boundary. The optional validate stage is disabled. After canonical evaluation, the strict gate admits Candidate only if its Validation 22 Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution score exceeds that of the matched Parent. The record operator retains outcomes and the revision rationale. Unlike AHE and the initial HyperAgents policy, A-Evolve combines greedy Parent choice with score-improving admission. A.4. GEPA Selection and Reflection. GEPA combines trajectory-based reflection with per-task Pareto selection (Agrawal et al., 2026). The select operator identifies eligible Candidates attaining the best observed score on at least one task, prunes redundant coverage, and samples according to the remaining per-task memberships. This can preserve access to task specialists without selecting solely by aggregate score. The rollout operator collects fresh Train trajectories, and analyze assembles task examples, outputs, and feedback for focused reflection. Revision Scope. The named reflection units differ by benchmark. On τ3-Banking, MiniSWE focuses on its system-prompt configuration, while Codex alternates between its prompt and taskexecution skill. On Terminal-Bench 2, both harnesses use the entire target as the reflection unit. These units guide evidence organization rather than impose text-only filesystem permissions. The frozen Champion from MiniSWE with GEPA on Terminal-Bench 2 retains inner-source changes to taskconditioned guidance and shell execution. Reflection-centric therefore describes the revision process, not the absence of code changes. These reflection units are distinct from the post-hoc Components isolated in our diagnostics. Validation and Admission. The validate operator evaluates the proposal on the same Train task batch used for the Parent rollout and requires complete, scorable comparison with strict improvement. This feedback-informed proposal filter precedes canonical Validation evaluation. The subsequent gate checks completion and eligibility without imposing second Parent-relative improvement threshold. The record operator preserves reflection choices, proposals, and batch comparisons. Thus, GEPAs improvement filter lies in validate, whereas A-Evolves lies in gate, and they use different task evidence. Implications for the Analysis. These implementations differ in how they allocate search, summarize evidence, couple target and operator changes, and filter proposals. Similar final gains can therefore arise through different processes. These differences motivate diagnostics of selection, diagnosis, change compatibility, and admission. B. Section B.4.1 provides the numerical cost table, and Section B.5 contains the split-level heatmaps. B.1. Matched Outcome Comparisons Evaluation and Interpretation. Every configuration in Table 1 uses the same benchmark tasks and eight complete passes. Each of the eight Champions per benchmark is paired with its harness Seed. The completed comparison contains 7,760 selected τ3-Banking executions and 7,120 TerminalBench 2 executions, including the two Seeds once per benchmark. Across the sixteen Champions, eleven improve reliability and ten improve coverage. Eight improve both, four move the metrics in opposite directions, one 23 Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution improves reliability with unchanged coverage, and three reduce both. The opposite-sign cases occur in reflection-centric general-task evolution and implementation-centric coding-task evolution, each with both harness types. Thus, the distinction between consistency and reach is not confined to one harness type, task domain, or paradigm, even though agreement is more common than disagreement. Interpreting Trends Across Dimensions. Reliability improves in all eight implementation-centric lineages across harness types and task domains. In the reflection-centric group, it improves in three of four source-editable cases but none of the four outer-layer-only cases. The paradigm-level pattern is therefore harness-dependent. The shared combination of these movements explains why neither net coverage gain nor reliability gain summarizes preservation. Pass-Half Stability. The reported analysis contains 22 tasklineage comparisons with trace-linked behavioral evidence.
